title: HERA: Assessing an Autonomous Agent for Quantum Device Measurement
authors: Zachary W. Gomez, Nathan Bittner, Jordan T. McCourt, Qingrui Cao, Sandesh S. Kalantre, Benjamin H. Alexander, Zhiren Zheng, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Aaron Sharpe
abstract: Large language model agents have begun to carry out laboratory measurements, but their scientific conclusions are useful only if they hold up under scrutiny. Demonstrating this requires controlled studies because models are stochastic and the context a model is given steers its conclusions. Here we introduce HERA, an autonomous agent designed to carry out cryogenic transport measurements of quantum devices. HERA draws on a knowledge base curated by lab members that holds measurement protocols, software tools, and literature references. We assessed HERA with a blinded trial against an expert on the stacking order of two multilayer graphene devices, an ablation of its knowledge base, and hundreds of offline replays in which models designed the trial's central measurement without running it. HERA's conclusions matched the expert's sealed conclusions on both tested devices. The ablation and the replay studies measured the impact of the knowledge base across different models, showing that with it every model designed better measurements and reasoned more soundly. To test how readily HERA extends to a new problem, we tasked it with finding and characterizing superconductivity in a different material system. This required a few hours of expert time to develop a new experimental protocol, after which HERA did both autonomously. These results show that, with a knowledge base designed for the task, language model agents are capable of sound experimental science.
summary: This paper introduces HERA, an autonomous AI agent designed to conduct complex, multi-step quantum device measurements in a cryogenic lab setting. By integrating a curated knowledge base, HERA was tested on determining graphene stacking order and finding superconductivity in new materials. The results show that LLM agents can perform sound, expert-level experimental science when properly scaffolded with domain knowledge.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of automating complex, multi-step experimental science, specifically cryogenic transport measurements on quantum devices, using autonomous AI agents.
main_result: The developed agent, HERA, successfully replicated expert conclusions in blinded trials for determining graphene stacking order and characterizing superconductivity in novel materials, demonstrating sound experimental capability when provided with a curated knowledge base.
method: The authors designed and tested HERA, an autonomous agent that uses a structured knowledge base (corpus) to write and execute code in live Jupyter notebooks for measurement and analysis, mimicking the scientific workflow.
model_or_system: The experiments are performed on atomically thin quantum devices, such as multilayer graphene and WSe2-proximitized bilayer graphene, measured under cryogenic conditions. The core 'model' is the HERA LLM agent, which interacts with the physical measurement setup and the curated scientific knowledge base.
key_observables: Shubnikov–de Haas (SdH) oscillation frequencies, carrier mass, critical current ($I_c$), superconducting transition temperature ($T_c$), and coherence length ($\xi_{GL}$).
important_parameters: Carrier density ($n$), magnetic field ($B$), temperature ($T$), and displacement field ($D/\epsilon_0$).
main_assumptions: The agent's performance is highly dependent on the quality, completeness, and structure of the human-curated knowledge base (corpus).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate HERA's architecture, measurement sequences for stacking order (showing $R$ vs $1/B$), and superconducting characterization plots ($R_{xx}$ vs $n$, $dV/dI$ vs $B$). Tables quantify agreement between HERA's conclusions and expert judgments.
paper_structure: The paper introduces HERA, details its components (knowledge base, notebooks), presents results from blinded prospective trials (stacking order), and then extends the assessment to a new physical problem (superconductivity) using multiple measurement sessions.
why_interesting: While the physics is condensed matter, the core contribution is the methodology—using LLMs to perform structured, verifiable scientific reasoning in a physical measurement context—which is highly relevant for future automated quantum characterization.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks
